# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform

Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).

## Architecture

- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).

## Portals & design system

**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.

- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).

- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).

- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.

- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).

## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session

`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.

1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).
4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.

If two sessions are likely to be editing at once, coordinate the ordinary way: pull before starting, small commits, push often (the auto-push hook does this for you on commit).

## Integrations (activate via /opt/nxeon/.env)

- **Stripe**: `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` + `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` → wallet top-ups switch from demo gateway to Checkout (`/api/stripe/checkout`, webhook `/api/stripe/webhook`, event `checkout.session.completed`, idempotent by session id). 21	 * the client is regenerated.
22	 */
23	import { termDiscountPct } from "./billing-terms";
24	
25	/** A row that MAY carry the intro columns (present at runtime, absent from stale types). */
26	type PlanIntroFields = { introPriceCents?: number | null; introTermMonths?: number | null };
27	
28	/**
29	 * The plan's intro MONTHLY price in cents, or null when it is unset, malformed, or
30	 * NOT genuinely below the regular price. Requiring `intro < regular` means a bad /
31	 * equal / higher value can never quietly RAISE the first-term charge — it just
32	 * disables the intro and the plan bills its regular price.
33	 *
34	 * `plan` is typed loose on the intro column because the symlinked prod Prisma client's
35	 * types predate it (regenerated at deploy); the value is present at runtime.
36	 */
37	export function planIntroMonthlyCents(plan: { priceCents: number }): number | null {
38	  const v = (plan as PlanIntroFields).introPriceCents;
39	  if (typeof v !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 0) return null;
40	  const cents = Math.round(v);
41	  if (cents >= plan.priceCents) return null;
42	  return cents;
43	}
44	
45	/**
46	 * How many of the first term's months are billed at the intro rate. NULL / invalid
47	 * => the WHOLE first term (returned as null so callers apply it across every month).
48	 * Clamped to >= 1 so a stray 0 can never zero the intro window. `plan` is `unknown`
49	 * for the same stale-client reason as above.
50	 */
51	export function planIntroTermMonths(plan: unknown): number | null {
52	  const v = (plan as PlanIntroFields | null | undefined)?.introTermMonths;
53	  if (typeof v !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 1) return null;
54	  return Math.round(v);
55	}
56	
57	/**
58	 * Cents knocked off the FIRST term because of the intro rate — 0 when there is no
59	 * intro. Expressed as a REDUCTION of the regular term total (not a second price)
60	 * so the regular term price stays the single source of truth and the renewal math
61	 * is untouched:
62	 *
63	 *   discount = (regularMonthly − introMonthly) × introMonths × (1 − termDiscount)
64	 *
65	 * `introMonths` is `min(introTermMonths ?? months, months)`, so a 1-month term is
66	 * fully intro-priced, and a "$3.99 first month" intro on a 12-month first order
67	 * discounts exactly one month and bills the other eleven at the regular rate.
68	 * The term discount is applied so the intro months are discounted consistently
69	 * with the rest of the term the customer chose.
70	 */
71	export function introFirstTermDiscountCents(
72	  regularMonthlyCents: number,
73	  introMonthlyCents: number | null,
74	  termMonths: number,
75	  introTermMonths: number | null,
76	  annualDiscountPct?: number,
77	): number {
78	  if (introMonthlyCents == null || introMonthlyCents >= regularMonthlyCents) return 0;
79	  const months = Math.max(1, Math.round(termMonths));
80	  const introMonths = introTermMonths != null ? Math.min(introTermMonths, months) : months;
81	  if (introMonths <= 0) return 0;
82	  const pct = termDiscountPct(months, annualDiscountPct);
83	  return Math.max(0, Math.round((regularMonthlyCents - introMonthlyCents) * introMonths * (1 - pct / 100)));
84	}
85	
86	/**
87	 * The percent OFF the regular term total that the intro first term represents,
88	 * as a whole number 0..100 — the value stamped on `Server.termPromoPercent` so
89	 * proration and refunds price against the rate the term was actually sold at.
90	 * Integer because it round-trips through Stripe metadata as an integer promo
91	 * percent (lib/order.ts parseOrderPrice), exactly like the seasonal promos.
92	 */
93	export function introSoldPercent(regularTermCents: number, introDiscountCents: number): number {
94	  if (regularTermCents <= 0 || introDiscountCents <= 0) return 0;
95	  return Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.round((introDiscountCents / regularTermCents) * 100)));
96	}

1	// Pure pricing + guardrail math for CUSTOM VPS / game-server specs — servers
2	// bigger than the biggest premade plan ("Max"). No DB, no server-only imports:
3	// this is the ONE formula shared by the client-side deploy wizards (instant price
4	// as a slider moves, no round trip) and the server-side quote/order path
5	// (lib/custom-plan.ts, which re-validates everything here before a Plan row is
6	// ever created — a client-computed price is never trusted for money).
7	//
8	// ─── WHY "CUSTOM" EXISTS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9	// The premade ladder tops out at Max (4 vCPU / 16 GB / 120 GB). A customer who
10	// needs more than that on ANY dimension gets a one-off Plan row sized exactly to
11	// what they asked for (see lib/custom-plan.ts createCustomPlan) instead of being
12	// turned away or overpaying for a fixed "XL" tier that's still too small. So a
13	// valid custom spec is, by definition, Max-or-bigger on every dimension and
14	// STRICTLY bigger on at least one — never a way to buy something Max-sized (or
15	// smaller) at a different price, which would undercut the catalog and break the
16	// price-monotonic / disk-monotonic invariants lib/resize.ts depends on to keep
17	// upgrades honest.
18	//
19	// ─── PRICING FORMULA DERIVATION ──────────────────────────────────────────────
20	// The live ladder (prisma — Plan table) and its price DELTAS between adjacent
21	// tiers:
22	//
23	//   Tier      vCPU  RAM(GB)  Disk(GB)  Price      Δ vCPU  Δ RAM  Δ Disk  Δ Price
24	//   Starter     1      2        25     $8.88
25	//   Standard    2      4        50    $12.99        1       2      25    411¢
26	//   Pro         3      8        80    $20.99        1       4      30    800¢
27	//   Max         4     16       120    $32.99        1       8      40   1200¢
28	//
29	// A pure 3-variable linear fit (price = a·Δvcpu + b·Δram_GB + c·Δdisk_GB) across
30	// those three deltas turns out to be OVER-determined in a way the real ladder
31	// can't satisfy exactly: solving any two of the three delta-equations for
32	// (a, b, c) and checking against the third leaves a residual (405¢ vs 800¢ i.e
33	// disk-GB deltas here are exactly `20*Δvcpu + 2.5*Δram_GB`, so the three price
34	// points don't sit on a single consistent (a,b,c) — there's no clean 3-variable
35	// exact solution, only a best fit). So rather than force an unstable joint
36	// regression across three highly-correlated columns (cpu/ram/disk all grow
37	// together tier-to-tier), we ANCHOR the disk rate to a number the platform
38	// already charges for exactly this resource — `extra_disk_gb_price_cents`
39	// (lib/disk-expand.ts / lib/settings.ts), the live $0.10/GB/month a customer on
40	// ANY premade plan already pays to add root disk beyond their plan's included
41	// amount. Reusing it here means a GB of disk costs the same $ whether it comes
42	// from the extra-disk upsell or from building a custom plan — one number, one
43	// meaning, platform-wide.
44	//
45	// With disk fixed at that rate (10¢/GB), each tier-to-tier price delta minus its
46	// disk contribution attributes the REMAINDER to cpu + ram:
47	//
48	//   Standard-Starter: 411 - 10·25 = 161 = 1a + 2b
49	//   Pro-Standard:      800 - 10·30 = 500 = 1a + 4b
50	//   Max-Pro:          1200 - 10·40 = 800 = 1a + 8b
51	//
52	// Least-squares fit of those three (a, b) equations (normal equations
53	// 3a+14b=1461, 14a+84b=8722) solves EXACTLY to a = 11, b = 102 — i.e. $0.11 per
54	// extra vCPU/month and $1.02 per extra GB RAM/month. (RAM dominates the ladder's
55	// price growth far more than CPU does, which matches lib/capacity.ts's own
56	// framing of RAM as "the scarce resource" the platform oversells carefully
57	// while CPU is comparatively cheap to add.)
58	//
59	// All three rates are admin-tunable via lib/settings.ts (`custom_plan_per_vcpu_cents`,
60	// `custom_plan_per_ram_gb_cents`; disk reuses the existing `extra_disk_gb_price_cents`)
61	// so the catalog can be retuned without a redeploy if the premade ladder ever moves.
62	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_DEFAULT_RATES: CustomPlanRates = {
63	  perVcpuCents: 11,
64	  perRamGbCents: 102,
65	  perDiskGbCents: 10, // mirrors extra_disk_gb_price_cents's shipped default
66	};
67	
68	/** Sane platform-wide ceiling — deliberately generous (nothing in the premade
69	 *  catalog approaches this), but not infinite: a real physical node has to be
70	 *  able to hold it. Admin-tunable via lib/settings.ts (custom_plan_max_*). */
71	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_DEFAULT_CEILING: CustomPlanCeiling = {
72	  maxCpuCores: 32,
73	  maxRamMB: 128 * 1024,
74	  maxDiskGB: 2000,
75	};
76	
77	/**
78	 * The `sortOrder` every one-off custom `Plan`/`GamePlan` row is created with (see
79	 * lib/custom-plan.ts). Shared here — a pure, dependency-free constant — so
80	 * lib/order.ts and lib/game-order.ts can recognize "this specific row is an
81	 * intentionally-inactive custom one-off, not a retired/disabled plan" without
82	 * either of them importing the DB-touching lib/custom-plan.ts. See the doc
83	 * comment on their `active` gates for why this matters: a custom plan is created
84	 * `active: false` so it stays invisible to the 30+ existing `where: { active: true }`
85	 * catalog/marketing/resize-picker queries across this codebase (none of which are
86	 * scoped to a single order or customer) — but it must still be a valid PURCHASE
87	 * TARGET for the one order that just built it.
88	 */
89	export const CUSTOM_PLAN_SORT_ORDER = 999;
90	
91	export type CustomPlanSpec = { cpuCores: number; ramMB: number; diskGB: number };
92	
93	/** The floor a custom spec must clear on every dimension — today, the live "Max"
94	 *  plan's specs (see lib/custom-plan.ts customPlanFloor, which reads it from the
95	 *  DB rather than hardcoding it, so a future catalog change is picked up live). */
96	export type CustomPlanFloor = {
97	  cpuCores: number;
98	  ramMB: number;
99	  diskGB: number;
100	  priceCents: number;
101	  bandwidthTB: number;
102	};
103	
104	export type CustomPlanCeiling = { maxCpuCores: number; maxRamMB: number; maxDiskGB: number };
105	
106	export type CustomPlanRates = { perVcpuCents: number; perRamGbCents: number; perDiskGbCents: number };
107	
108	/**
109	 * The custom-plan price: Max's price plus the per-unit rate for whatever exceeds
110	 * Max on each dimension. Only the EXCESS over the floor is charged for — a spec
111	 * that matches Max on RAM/disk but asks for double the CPU pays only for the
112	 * extra CPU, not a second copy of Max's whole price.
113	 *
114	 * Defensively clamped to STRICTLY more than the floor's price: a valid spec
115	 * (per validateCustomPlanSpec) always exceeds the floor on at least one
116	 * dimension, so with positive rates this clamp is a no-op — but if an admin ever
117	 * zeroes a rate (e.g. sets `extra_disk_gb_price_cents` to "0"), a disk-only
118	 * custom spec must still never price at-or-below Max, which would silently
119	 * undercut the catalog (the exact class of bug lib/resize.ts's price-monotonic
120	 * guard exists to prevent one level up, at resize time).
121	 */
122	export function computeCustomPlanPriceCents(
123	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
124	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
125	  rates: CustomPlanRates,
126	): number {
127	  const extraCpu = Math.max(0, spec.cpuCores - floor.cpuCores);
128	  const extraRamGB = Math.max(0, (spec.ramMB - floor.ramMB) / 1024);
129	  const extraDiskGB = Math.max(0, spec.diskGB - floor.diskGB);
130	  const raw =
131	    floor.priceCents +
132	    extraCpu * rates.perVcpuCents +
133	    extraRamGB * rates.perRamGbCents +
134	    extraDiskGB * rates.perDiskGbCents;
135	  return Math.max(Math.round(raw), floor.priceCents + 1);
136	}
137	
138	/**
139	 * Guardrails: every dimension must be at or above the floor (never a way to buy
140	 * something Max-sized or smaller under a different name) and at or below the
141	 * admin-configured ceiling. A spec that matches the floor EXACTLY on all three
142	 * dimensions is rejected too — that's just Max, not a custom order.
143	 */
144	export function validateCustomPlanSpec(
145	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
146	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
147	  ceiling: CustomPlanCeiling,
148	): { ok: true } | { ok: false; reason: string } {
149	  if (!Number.isFinite(spec.cpuCores) || !Number.isFinite(spec.ramMB) || !Number.isFinite(spec.diskGB)) {
150	    return { ok: false, reason: "Invalid configuration." };
151	  }
152	  if (spec.cpuCores < floor.cpuCores || spec.ramMB < floor.ramMB || spec.diskGB < floor.diskGB) {
153	    return {
154	      ok: false,
155	      reason:
156	        `A custom server can't go below ${floor.cpuCores} vCPU / ${floor.ramMB / 1024} GB RAM / ${floor.diskGB} GB disk ` +
157	        `on any dimension — for anything smaller, pick a plan above instead.`,
158	    };
159	  }
160	  if (spec.cpuCores > ceiling.maxCpuCores || spec.ramMB > ceiling.maxRamMB || spec.diskGB > ceiling.maxDiskGB) {
161	    return {
162	      ok: false,
163	      reason:
164	        `Custom servers top out at ${ceiling.maxCpuCores} vCPU / ${ceiling.maxRamMB / 1024} GB RAM / ` +
165	        `${ceiling.maxDiskGB} GB disk — contact support for anything larger.`,
166	    };
167	  }
168	  if (spec.cpuCores === floor.cpuCores && spec.ramMB === floor.ramMB && spec.diskGB === floor.diskGB) {
169	    return { ok: false, reason: "That's exactly the Max plan — choose Max above instead of building custom." };
170	  }
171	  return { ok: true };
172	}
173	
174	/** Clamp an arbitrary (e.g. slider-dragged, or player-count-derived) spec into the
175	 *  floor..ceiling range, rounding to whole units. Used by the UI so a slider or a
176	 *  recommendation can never even VISUALLY suggest an invalid spec. */
177	export function clampCustomPlanSpec(
178	  spec: CustomPlanSpec,
179	  floor: CustomPlanFloor,
180	  ceiling: CustomPlanCeiling,
181	): CustomPlanSpec {
182	  return {
183	    cpuCores: Math.min(ceiling.maxCpuCores, Math.max(floor.cpuCores, Math.round(spec.cpuCores))),
184	    ramMB: Math.min(ceiling.maxRamMB, Math.max(floor.ramMB, Math.round(spec.ramMB))),
185	    diskGB: Math.min(ceiling.maxDiskGB, Math.max(floor.diskGB, Math.round(spec.diskGB))),
186	  };
187	}
188	
189	/** Human name for the one-off Plan/GamePlan row this spec becomes. */
190	export function customPlanName(spec: CustomPlanSpec): string {
191	  const ramGB = Math.round(spec.ramMB / 1024);
192	  return `Custom ${spec.cpuCores} vCPU / ${ramGB} GB / ${spec.diskGB} GB Disk`;
193	}
194	
195	/** Slug pattern mirrors the one pre-existing manual precedent ("custom-4c8g-hmcebh")
196	 *  — short enough to stay under adminSavePlan's 30-char slug cap even at the
197	 *  ceiling's largest specs. `suffix` is a short random string the caller supplies
198	 *  (lib/custom-plan.ts) so this module stays free of any randomness/DB concerns. */
199	export function customPlanSlug(spec: CustomPlanSpec, suffix: string): string {
200	  const ramGB = Math.round(spec.ramMB / 1024);
201	  return `custom-${spec.cpuCores}c${ramGB}g-${suffix}`.slice(0, 30);
202	}

7	// Every family already has 2-3 REAL, shipped tiers in the catalog (prisma/

9	// ramMB/cpuCores/diskGB paired with a player-slot count. Rather than invent numbers
10	// from scratch, each family's curve below is a least-squares linear fit

163	/** Slider ceiling per family: 5x the largest tier actually sold today, floored at
164	 *  50 so even a small-roster game (e.g. The Forest, seeded up to 8) still offers a
165	 *  meaningfully bigger custom option. */
166	export function playerSliderMax(family: GameFamily): number {
167	  const c = GAME_PLAYER_CURVES[family];
168	  return Math.max(50, c.maxSeededSlots * 5);
169	}
170	
171	/**
172	 * Recommended cpu/ram/disk for a given player count on this family — a
173	 * DEFAULT-SETTER for the custom-spec sliders, never a hard floor or ceiling
174	 * itself (the caller clamps into the actual custom-plan floor/ceiling).
175	 */
176	export function recommendedSpecForPlayers(family: GameFamily, players: number): GameResourceSpec {
177	  const c = GAME_PLAYER_CURVES[family];
178	  const p = Math.max(1, Math.round(players));
179	  const ramMB = Math.max(512, Math.round((c.ramBaseMB + c.ramPerPlayerMB * p) / 256) * 256);
180	  const cpuCores = Math.max(1, Math.round(c.cpuBaseCores + c.cpuPerPlayer * p));
181	  const diskGB = Math.max(5, Math.round(c.diskBaseGB + c.diskPerPlayerGB * p));
182	  return { cpuCores, ramMB, diskGB };
183	}

# Nxeon — VPS hosting platform

Hostinger-style VPS hosting platform running on this Proxmox VE 9 dedicated server (OVH KS-GAME, i7-7700K, 64GB RAM, 2×450GB NVMe ZFS mirror + 4TB HDD backup pool).

## Architecture

- **Web panel**: Next.js 15 (App Router, server actions) + Tailwind v4, served by `nxeon-web.service` on port 3000, behind nginx on port 80. Public IP: 51.79.162.96.
- **Worker**: `worker/index.ts` run by `nxeon-worker.service` (as root — it manages iptables). Polls the `Job` table every 3s and executes provisioning/lifecycle jobs against the Proxmox API.
- **DB**: PostgreSQL 17, database `nxeon`, Prisma ORM ([prisma/schema.prisma](prisma/schema.prisma)). Use `npm run db:push` after schema changes.
- **Proxmox**: API token auth (`nxeon@pve!platform`, creds in `.env`). Templates: VMID 9000 (Ubuntu 24.04), 9001 (Debian 13), cloud-init based, cloned onto ZFS storage `vmdata`.
- **Networking**: VMs attach to NAT bridge `vmbr1` (10.20.0.0/24, gateway .1). IPs allocated from 10.20.0.100–250 ([lib/ipam.ts](lib/ipam.ts)). SSH exposed via DNAT port forwards 20000–29999 in iptables chain `NXEON_FWD`, rebuilt from DB by [worker/network.ts](worker/network.ts) — never edit that chain by hand.
- **Cloud-init**: vendor snippet at `/tank/backup/snippets/nxeon-vendor.yaml` (installs qemu-guest-agent, enables root password SSH).

## Portals & design system

**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.

- **Two portals, two shells, deliberately unmerged:**
  - `app/admin/**` (admin ops portal) still renders through `components/portal/Shell.tsx` — the ORIGINAL, pre-redesign chrome. Marketing (`app/(marketing)/**`), `/login`, `/register` and admin must stay pixel-identical to how they looked before the redesign. Never edit these expecting Nexion's visual language to apply, and never move Nexion-only styling into a place they can see it.
  - `app/dashboard/**` (customer portal) renders through `components/nx/Shell.tsx` — the Nexion redesign. This is where the new design system, its components (`components/nx/*`), and its color/animation language live.
  - **A component added to one shell must be added to the other if it's meant to exist on both.** This has silently broken things before: `ComposeProvider`, `TerminalDockProvider`, `MatrixProvider` were each added to `components/portal/Shell.tsx` first and forgotten on `components/nx/Shell.tsx`, taking a whole feature down invisibly (the crash only appeared on a route a smoke test didn't walk).

- **The scoping trick that keeps the two visually separate — `app/globals.css`, `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)`:**
  Nexion's own colors/tokens and its overrides of shared component classes (`.card`, `.btn-primary`, `.input`, etc.) are NOT bare rules — they're wrapped in `:root:has(.nx-shell-root) { ... }`, a selector that only matches when a `.nx-shell-root` element (rendered only by `components/nx/Shell.tsx`) exists anywhere on the page. That's the entire mechanism keeping marketing/login/admin rendering their original, pre-redesign styles: **do not write a new bare rule for a class both portals share** (e.g. a bare `.card { ... }` outside this scope) — it will apply everywhere, including where it was never meant to.
  - Light mode has its own nested scope for the same reason: `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)[data-theme="light"]`, NOT a bare `html[data-theme="light"]`. The bare form loses a CSS specificity fight to the dark `:has()` block regardless of which theme is active — this was a real, session-spanning bug (several "light mode doesn't work on page X" reports all had this one root cause) before it was scoped correctly.
  - `.nx-dark-island` is a third scope, deliberately staying dark inside the Nexion portal even when light mode is active (site headers, page hero banners) — it re-declares the relevant tokens back to dark values inside `html[data-theme="light"] .nx-dark-island { ... }`. Add a new always-dark token here too if you introduce one (see `--color-neon-bug` for the pattern: declared in the base `@theme` block, overridden lighter in the light-mode scope, re-declared back to its bright value inside `.nx-dark-island`).

- **CSS/JS landmines hit (and fixed) building this — avoid repeating them:**
  - **`@keyframes` and `@property` are not valid nested inside a plain style rule** — only inside `@layer`/`@media`/other at-rules. Nesting one inside `:root:has(...) { }` (or any class selector) silently drops it at build time — no error, the animation just never plays, forever, with every other signal (computed `animation-name`, `animation-play-state: running`) looking correct. This broke ~34 animations at once (a levitating icon, the page preloader, several status dots) when a broad `:has()` refactor accidentally wrapped them. If an animation looks "stuck on frame one," check whether its `@keyframes` block ended up nested inside a style rule.
  - **`backdrop-filter` on an ancestor creates a new containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.** A `.card` with `backdrop-blur-md` breaks any non-portaled modal/overlay nested inside it (it pins to the card instead of the viewport). Fix: cancel the inherited `backdrop-filter` on the offending class, or `createPortal` the fixed element to `document.body`.
  - **A positioned `fixed; z-0` decorative background (an aurora/globe effect) paints above ordinary static content** unless the real content wrapper gets `relative z-[1]`.
  - **Hydration-mismatch anti-pattern**: `useState(() => { if (typeof window === "undefined") return X; ...read window/URL...; return Y; })` — the server always takes the `X` branch, the client's first render always takes `Y`, guaranteed mismatch. Read the value server-side (a Server Component's `searchParams` prop) and pass it down as a real prop instead.
  - Percentage-based `transform: translateY(%)` inside a flex item whose container has no defined width/height resolves against 0 and silently does nothing — give the container a real dimension (e.g. `inset-0` instead of `inset-y-0 right-0` alone) before debugging the animation itself.
  - `git commit -m` with backticks in the message breaks — write the message to a file and use `git commit -F`.
  - Bash `cwd` does not persist between tool calls in an agent session — always `cd /opt/nxeon && ...` in the same command.

- Design system tokens/classes live in `app/globals.css` + `components/ui/primitives.tsx` (shared/production) and `components/nx/*` (Nexion-only). Charts are dependency-free SVG (`components/ui/charts.tsx`) — do not add a charting library.
- Admin impersonation: `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target, `realUser()` the actual admin; banner + exit handled in Shell. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireAdmin` and refuse to render while impersonating.
- Metrics come from Proxmox RRD via `/api/metrics` (node for admins, per-server for owners). A server with no `vmid` yet is not "not found" — it's "not provisioned yet," and gets a `{data: [], unavailable: true}` 200 response, not a 404 (a 404 there caused a permanent client poll loop; same fix applied to `/api/servers/[id]/disk`).

## Working on this codebase — one tree, any session

`/opt/nxeon` (this directory, branch `main`) is the single source of truth. There is no longer a required separate sandbox for ordinary changes — the node-2 box (`/opt/nxeon-v2`) that incubated the Nexion redesign still exists and is safe to use for a large, risky, or highly iterative piece of work (it runs sandboxed: `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` stubs Proxmox provisioning and Stripe charges), but is optional, not a gate. Any session — this one or another — can edit `main` directly and ship through the pipeline below.

1. Edit, then `npx tsc --noEmit` before building anything.
2. `npm run build` locally only to catch build errors before pushing — do not restart production services from an ad hoc build in this directory (see Commands below); this is validation, not deployment.
3. Commit (small, real commits — the GitHub post-commit hook auto-pushes `origin`).

I'm gathering competitor Minecraft hosting pricing benchmarks, noting per-GB rates for Shockbyte, Apex, and GGServers hover around $2.80-3.75/GB depending on tier.

Checking a few more providers - HostHavoc, SparkedHost, PebbleHost, GPORTAL, and Nitrado - confirms budget hosts sit near $1/GB while premium slot-based hosts like Nitrado run up to $8/GB. Nxeon's current pricing lands in the mid-competitive range around $2.88-3.59/GB, which looks solid.

With this benchmark data in hand, I'm shifting to the design phase, recognizing this is a large task spanning 47 families and roughly 188 tiers, so I need an efficient, systematic approach: for each family I'll work from existing tier specs (RAM, CPU, disk, slots, pricing) to determine what new tiers are needed.

Six families (cs2, palworld, sonsoftheforest, terraria, theforest, valheim) currently have only 2 tiers and need 2 new ones each, while the remaining 41 families have 3 tiers and need just 1 additional tier apiece — I'm now working through where each new tier should sit relative to existing ones.

Existing tiers stay fixed, so new tiers must be added without disturbing current ids, specs, or prices, and each game's real minimum RAM requirement sets a floor for how low an entry tier can go. For families that can't support a cheaper entry tier, the instructions say to add two tiers above the top instead of one below, so I need to go family by family and decide whether a budget tier fits or whether it's better to extend the ladder upward.

Going through the rest of the family list, most of these are heavier games with substantial RAM floors already, so dropping the entry tier further risks instability. A better approach might be offering a reduced-player-count "starter" version of the existing lowest tier rather than lowering RAM itself.

Looking at real hosting practices, Rust's existing 4GB tier is already near the practical floor, so instead of going lower I should add a higher-end tier like 16GB for larger populations, while ARK's lowest existing tier of 8GB seems reasonable to keep as-is.

Actually, the constraint is about overall minimum requirement, not per-player-count — as long as it genuinely runs a small Ark server, a lower tier is legitimate, and real hosts like Nitrado do sell 4GB ARK plans. Given the scope of this task, I should settle on a consistent, defensible policy for tier placement documented in my methodology, rather than trying to recall exact real-world minimums for every single game from memory, since that risks fabrication. The instructions do allow adding a smaller entry tier and/or larger top tier flexibly depending on each game's constraints.

For each family, I'll use the resource curves grounded in real specs to estimate requirements at a realistic low player count, and if that comes out meaningfully lower (~25%+) than the current lowest tier and rounds cleanly, I'll add a new entry tier sized and priced by extrapolating the family's own per-GB pricing curve downward.

But for families where the lowest tier already sits near a practical floor -- below curve minimums, common absolute minimums like 1GB, or engine-imposed RAM floors (often 4GB+ for survival games) -- I'll skip adding a lower tier since it wouldn't make sense.

For the top side, I'm considering adding a new tier above the current highest, sized for a larger player count, and extending moderately beyond the current cap since the slider already allows generous extrapolation. For the six families needing two new tiers, I'll add one below and one above where feasible, or stack both on the side that's actually extensible.

Rather than working through all 47 tiers narratively, I'm planning to write a script to compute suggested tier specs using the recommendation curves, plus a pricing model fitting price to RAM linearly based on existing data points. Checking minecraft's pricing as an example, I find a rough slope of about $264 per GB with a $190 base offset, which approximates the actual tiers reasonably well.

The script would load existing tiers per family, fit price-vs-RAM curves using least squares (matching the codebase's existing methodology), and do the same for intro pricing or fall back to a consistent intro-to-regular ratio. It would decide whether new tiers go below or above existing ones by comparing curve-computed RAM against current lowest tier thresholds, then assign reasonable player counts for new entry tiers based on a percentage of the existing lowest tier's capacity.

I'll snap RAM to the nearest nice value from a predefined ladder of GB values, then derive CPU cores and disk size from the curve as well, cross-checking against the base plan selection to pick the smallest active match.

For pricing, I'll use the linear fit but sanity check it against neighboring tiers and the family's own $/GB curve, since that's the primary anchor rather than hard-coded competitor numbers — I'll just reference the Shockbyte/GGServers/PebbleHost/HostHavoc benchmarks in the narrative. For the intro price on new entry tiers, I'll apply the same discount fraction as the family's smaller tiers use.

Some families (armareforger, ats, cs16, dayz, ets2) have no intro pricing at all across their tiers — those wave 10/11 additions seem to have launched without it entirely. So I'll stay consistent: if all existing tiers in a family have intro pricing, add it to the new tier at the same ratio; if the family has no intro pricing anywhere, skip it for the new tier too.

For featured flags, I'll leave existing tiers untouched since the task only says specs/price must stay unchanged, and I'll just mark all new tiers as featured=false to keep things simple and safe. For sortOrder, I'm appending new tiers at the end, unless one needs to become the new lowest entry tier, in which case I'd shift the others up by one.

That's actually the clean solution — use a negative sortOrder like -1 for a new entry tier so it sorts first without touching existing rows, and use max+1 (e.g. 3) for a new top tier. I should verify that existing sortOrders are contiguous starting at 0 across families before relying on this pattern.

Since the task says "upsert by id" but these are brand new rows with no existing id, I need to mint a deterministic id string myself (like `gp-<family>-<tierslug>`) in the seed script rather than letting Prisma generate a cuid, so re-running the script upserts the same row instead of duplicating it.

I'll mint deterministic ids for every row this script touches, rather than reusing prod's random cuids, since that keeps things semantically clear and idempotent — something like `seed4t-<family>-<tierKey>`. For families already in staging with baseline tiers seeded elsewhere, my script should only add the missing new tiers rather than duplicating the existing baseline ones.

For families that already have tiers in staging, I'll upsert only the new tiers by deterministic id, leaving baseline rows untouched. For the 5 families entirely new to staging, I need to insert all 4 tiers (3 baseline plus 1 new) with deterministic ids too — since nothing exists there yet, this doesn't violate the "keep existing tiers unchanged" rule, it's just populating parity with prod as intended.

I also need matching OsTemplate rows for those 5 families, which I'll upsert by unique slug rather than hardcoding ids. For basePlanId, I'll query staging's Plan table dynamically instead of hardcoding, since staging's Starter/Standard/Pro/Max plans have different ids than prod despite matching RAM tiers, following the seed-gameplans.ts convention.

Now the bulk of the actual work: for each of the 47 families I need to decide direction (entry vs top vs both) and the new tier's specs — players, ram, cpu, disk, price, introPrice. Given the scale, I'll build a script with programmatic rules, spot-check a sample manually, and document any exceptions where four tiers didn't make sense.

I'll compute the numbers with a separate helper script, but ultimately hardcode the final chosen tiers into the seed script as an explicit array, matching repo convention and letting me hand-tune outliers. The direction rule looks at existing tiers sorted by RAM, then derives an entry-tier player count as roughly half the lowest tier's slots (with a sane minimum), mapping that to a recommended spec via the player curves.

For entry tiers, I add one only if the curve-derived RAM is meaningfully lower (at least 25% less) and rounds to a distinct nice GB value; otherwise I check whether a top tier is warranted by testing a higher player count (roughly 1.6x the current max, capped by the curve's max seeded slots) and adding a TOP tier if its RAM requirement exceeds the current highest tier's.

Rather than manually reasoning through all 47 families, I'll write a quick script that imports the app's own player-curve function, computes these numbers for every family, and prints a table I can then finalize by hand with pricing and rounding judgment—this keeps the specs grounded in the app's real logic instead of guesswork.

content.thinking:
I've settled on a final list of 53 rows, and now I'm planning the seed script that builds the tier structure, working out how sortOrder should be calculated for entry versus top-tier positions within each family.

I want the sortOrder logic to be computed dynamically by querying existing active tier counts and max sortOrder per family, rather than hardcoded, so it stays correct across different database states — including the five missing families that need baseline tiers inserted first before the new one goes at sortOrder 3. Now I'm sketching the actual seed logic: iterating over each family, first ensuring baseline tiers exist via deterministic upsert IDs for the five missing families, then inserting the new tiers with correctly computed sortOrders.

For entry-direction tiers, sortOrder is always -1 since no family ever has two entries. For top-direction tiers I need to handle the distinction between a first new top and a second new top, since some families (cs2, palworld, sonsoftheforest, terraria, theforest, valheim) get both a "top" and "top2" tier and their sortOrders must be sequential based on what already exists in that family.

Ah, I see it now — that "top2" label is just a cosmetic artifact of my script counting the second processed item per family, not an indication of two top tiers. Only cs2 actually has two genuine top tiers since it lacks an entry tier; the others (palworld, sonsoftheforest, terraria, theforest, valheim) each have just one entry + one top, so I should rename their single top tier's id to drop the misleading "2" suffix.

For sortOrder, I'll compute it dynamically in the seed script by querying existing tiers per family before inserting new ones — for the single-top families that means sortOrder 2 continuing from existing 0,1, while cs2 gets its two new top tiers at sortOrder 2 and 3.

Since baseline insertion runs first, by the time I process new tiers the query will correctly see the existing tiers already in the DB for those families. I need to handle multiple top tiers per family by tracking a running sortOrder counter, and I'll set featured to false for all new tiers so the owner can review and toggle them later.

For the remaining fields: termMonths=1 to match existing convention, active=true so they're visible for staging review, and introTermMonths=null since none of the sampled existing tiers had a non-null value.

Now I'll move on to writing the seed script for the four-tier GamePlans.

 * script is the other half: one NEW tier per family (two for the handful that
 * only had 2), added on top of the untouched existing ladder.

 * DESIGN RULES (see /root/nxeon-competitive/plan-ladders.md for the full
 * per-family table + method):
 *   - Every existing tier's id/specs/price is left COMPLETELY alone — this
 *     script only INSERTS new rows, it never updates an existing GamePlan.
 *   - Each new tier is sized off lib/game-player-recommend.ts's own fitted
 *     player→resource curve for that family (the same curve the live deploy
 *     wizard/custom-plan slider already uses), snapped to a "nice" RAM value.
 *   - A smaller ENTRY tier is added below the current floor wherever the
 *     curve says that's a real, runnable size for the game; where the
 *     existing floor is already the practical minimum (or the curve is a
 *     placeholder — see the SCAFFOLD note below), a bigger TOP tier is added
 *     instead. Families that only had 2 tiers get one of each.
 *   - New-tier price is fit from the family's OWN existing price-vs-RAM
 *     tiers (linear regression), floored so a smaller entry tier is never
 *     cheaper per-GB than the smallest existing tier (a raw 2-3-point linear
 *     extrapolation can go negative-intercept and imply the opposite).
 *   - `slots` on every new tier is a RECOMMENDATION, not a cap — see the

async function main() {
  const plans = await db.plan.findMany({ where: { active: true }, orderBy: { ramMB: "asc" } });
  if (plans.length === 0) {
    throw new Error("No active VPS plans found — run the main seed first (npx prisma db seed).");
  }
  const largestPlan = plans[plans.length - 1];

  function pickBasePlan(ramMB: number) {
    return plans.find((p) => p.ramMB >= ramMB) ?? largestPlan;
  }

  async function pickOsTemplate(gameFamily: string): Promise<string | null> {
    const os = await db.osTemplate.findFirst({
      where: { family: gameFamily, category: "APPLICATION" },
      orderBy: { sortOrder: "asc" },
    });
    return os?.id ?? null;
  }

  // ── Step 1: create any missing OsTemplate rows (upsert by slug) ──────────
  let osCreated = 0;
  for (const [family, spec] of Object.entries(MISSING_OS_TEMPLATES)) {
    const existing = await db.osTemplate.findUnique({ where: { slug: spec.slug } });
    if (existing) continue;
    await db.osTemplate.create({ data: spec });
    osCreated++;
    console.log(`  [os] created OsTemplate for ${family} (was missing on this database)`);
  }

  // ── Step 2: copy baseline tiers for families staging never got ───────────
  let baselineCreated = 0;
  let baselineUpdated = 0;
  for (const spec of BASELINE_FOR_MISSING_FAMILIES) {
    const basePlan = pickBasePlan(spec.ramMB);
    const osId = await pickOsTemplate(spec.gameFamily);
    const data = {
      gameFamily: spec.gameFamily,
      name: spec.name,
      ramMB: spec.ramMB,
      cpuCores: spec.cpuCores,
      diskGB: spec.diskGB,
      slots: spec.slots,
      priceCents: spec.priceCents,
      introPriceCents: spec.introPriceCents,
      introTermMonths: null,
      termMonths: 1,
      basePlanId: basePlan.id,
      osTemplateId: osId,
      featured: spec.sortOrder === 1, // matches prod's convention (middle tier featured)
      active: true,
      sortOrder: spec.sortOrder,
    };
    const existing = await db.gamePlan.findUnique({ where: { id: spec.id } });
    if (existing) {
      await db.gamePlan.update({ where: { id: spec.id }, data });
      baselineUpdated++;
    } else {
      await db.gamePlan.create({ data: { id: spec.id, ...data } });
      baselineCreated++;
    }
  }

  // ── Step 3: add the new 4th (or 3rd+4th) tier for every family ───────────
  let tierCreated = 0;
  let tierUpdated = 0;
  for (const spec of NEW_TIERS) {
    const basePlan = pickBasePlan(spec.ramMB);
    const osId = await pickOsTemplate(spec.gameFamily);
    // sortOrder: entry tiers sort before every existing tier (existing ones
    // are never renumbered — see the "only ADD tiers" rule above); top tiers
    // sort after every currently-active tier for this family, in the order
    // NEW_TIERS lists them (matters for cs2's two new top tiers).
    let sortOrder: number;
    if (spec.direction === "entry") {
      sortOrder = -1;
    } else {
      const agg = await db.gamePlan.aggregate({
        where: { gameFamily: spec.gameFamily, active: true, id: { not: spec.id } },
        _max: { sortOrder: true },
      });
      sortOrder = (agg._max.sortOrder ?? -1) + 1;
    }
    const data = {
      gameFamily: spec.gameFamily,
      name: spec.name,
      ramMB: spec.ramMB,
      cpuCores: spec.cpuCores,
      diskGB: spec.diskGB,
      slots: spec.slots,
      priceCents: spec.priceCents,
      introPriceCents: spec.introPriceCents,
      introTermMonths: null,
      termMonths: 1,
      basePlanId: basePlan.id,
      osTemplateId: osId,
      featured: false, // new tiers ship unfeatured; owner can promote after review
      active: true,
      sortOrder,
    };
    const existing = await db.gamePlan.findUnique({ where: { id: spec.id } });
    if (existing) {
      await db.gamePlan.update({ where: { id: spec.id }, data });
      tierUpdated++;
    } else {
      await db.gamePlan.create({ data: { id: spec.id, ...data } });
      tierCreated++;
    }
    console.log(
      `  ${spec.gameFamily.padEnd(16)} ${spec.name.padEnd(46)} → base=${basePlan.name} img=${osId ? "yes" : "auto"} sortOrder=${sortOrder}`,
    );
  }

  console.log(`\nOsTemplate rows created: ${osCreated}`);
  console.log(`Baseline (missing-family) tiers: ${baselineCreated} created, ${baselineUpdated} updated`);
  console.log(`New 4th-tier rows: ${tierCreated} created, ${tierUpdated} updated`);

  // ── Verify: every family now has exactly 4 active tiers ──────────────────
  const counts = await db.gamePlan.groupBy({
    by: ["gameFamily"],
    where: { active: true },
    _count: { _all: true },
  });
  const notFour = counts.filter((c) => c._count._all !== 4);
  console.log(`\nFamilies with active tiers: ${counts.length}`);
  if (notFour.length > 0) {
    console.log("Families NOT at exactly 4 active tiers:");
    for (const c of notFour) console.log(`  ${c.gameFamily}: ${c._count._all}`);
  } else {
    console.log("Every family has exactly 4 active tiers. ✔");
  }
}

main()
  .catch((e) => {
    console.error(e);
    process.exit(1);
  })
  .finally(async () => {
    await db.$disconnect();
  });

/**
 * 4-TIER LADDER + CUSTOM-OPTION PARITY (2026-09-27)
 *
 * Owner ask: every game family gets 4 plans instead of today's 2-3, plus a
 * custom-server option, with player counts framed as RECOMMENDATIONS (server
 * sizing), never hard limits. The custom option already exists platform-wide
 * (lib/custom-plan.ts createCustomGamePlan, wired into GameDeployWizard) — this
 * script is the other half: one NEW tier per family (two for the handful that
 * only had 2), added on top of the untouched existing ladder.
 *
 * DESIGN RULES (see /root/nxeon-competitive/plan-ladders.md for the full
 * per-family table + method):
 *   - Every existing tier's id/specs/price is left COMPLETELY alone — this
 *     script only INSERTS new rows, it never updates an existing GamePlan.
 *   - Each new tier is sized off lib/game-player-recommend.ts's own fitted
 *     player→resource curve for that family (the same curve the live deploy
 *     wizard/custom-plan slider already uses), snapped to a "nice" RAM value.
 *   - A smaller ENTRY tier is added below the current floor wherever the
 *     curve says that's a real, runnable size for the game; where the
 *     existing floor is already the practical minimum (or the curve is a
 *     placeholder — see the SCAFFOLD note below), a bigger TOP tier is added
 *     instead. Families that only had 2 tiers get one of each.
 *   - New-tier price is fit from the family's OWN existing price-vs-RAM
 *     tiers (linear regression), floored so a smaller entry tier is never
 *     cheaper per-GB than the smallest existing tier (a raw 2-3-point linear
 *     extrapolation can go negative-intercept and imply the opposite).
 *   - `slots` on every new tier is a RECOMMENDATION, not a cap — see the
 *     matching GameDeployWizard.tsx copy change ("Sized for ~N players")
 *     shipped in the same commit as this script.
 *
 * Five families exist in prod's catalog but are entirely missing from
 * staging (dayz, armareforger, cs16, ets2, ats) — their OsTemplate rows are
 * missing too. This script also creates those OsTemplate rows and copies
 * their 3 existing tiers VERBATIM (same specs/prices, fresh ids — ids are
 * per-database anyway) before adding each family's 4th tier, so staging
 * matches prod's catalogue shape everywhere.
 *
 * Idempotent: every row (new tier + missing-family baseline copy + OsTemplate)
 * is upserted by a deterministic id/slug, so re-running is always safe.
 *
 * Run against a specific database:
 *   DATABASE_URL="<staging-url>" npx tsx prisma/seed-gameplans-4tier.ts
 *
 * STAGING ONLY as of 2026-09-27 — do not point this at the production
 * DATABASE_URL without the owner's sign-off on prisma/plan-ladders.md's
 * prices (see that file's "to apply to production" line).
 */
import { PrismaClient } from "@prisma/client";

const db = new PrismaClient();

// ─── OsTemplate rows staging is missing entirely (copied verbatim from prod) ──
const MISSING_OS_TEMPLATES: Record<
  string,
  {
    slug: string; name: string; category: "APPLICATION"; family: string; version: string; logo: string;
    vmid: number; baseVmid: number | null; setupScript: string; minRamMB: number; minDiskGB: number;
    licenseRequired: boolean; featured: boolean; sortOrder: number; active: boolean;
  }
> = {
  armareforger: {
    slug: "armareforger", name: "Arma Reforger Server", category: "APPLICATION",

async function main() {
  const plans = await db.plan.findMany({ where: { active: true }, orderBy: { ramMB: "asc" } });
  if (plans.length === 0) {
    throw new Error("No active VPS plans found — run the main seed first (npx prisma db seed).");
  }
  const largestPlan = plans[plans.length - 1];

  function pickBasePlan(ramMB: number) {
    return plans.find((p) => p.ramMB >= ramMB) ?? largestPlan;
  }

  async function pickOsTemplate(gameFamily: string): Promise<string | null> {
    const os = await db.osTemplate.findFirst({
      where: { family: gameFamily, category: "APPLICATION" },
      orderBy: { sortOrder: "asc" },
    });
    return os?.id ?? null;
  }

  // ── Step 1: create any missing OsTemplate rows (upsert by slug) ──────────
  let osCreated = 0;
  for (const [family, spec] of Object.entries(MISSING_OS_TEMPLATES)) {
    const existing = await db.osTemplate.findUnique({ where: { slug: spec.slug } });
    if (existing) continue;
    await db.osTemplate.create({ data: spec });
    osCreated++;
    console.log(`  [os] created OsTemplate for ${family} (was missing on this database)`);
  }

  // ── Step 2: copy baseline tiers for families staging never got ───────────
  let baselineCreated = 0;
  let baselineUpdated = 0;
  for (const spec of BASELINE_FOR_MISSING_FAMILIES) {
    const basePlan = pickBasePlan(spec.ramMB);
    const osId = await pickOsTemplate(spec.gameFamily);
    const data = {
      gameFamily: spec.gameFamily,
      name: spec.name,
      ramMB: spec.ramMB,
      cpuCores: spec.cpuCores,
      diskGB: spec.diskGB,
      slots: spec.slots,
      priceCents: spec.priceCents,
      introPriceCents: spec.introPriceCents,
      introTermMonths: null,
      termMonths: 1,
      basePlanId: basePlan.id,
      osTemplateId: osId,
      featured: spec.sortOrder === 1, // matches prod's convention (middle tier featured)
      active: true,
      sortOrder: spec.sortOrder,
    };
    const existing = await db.gamePlan.findUnique({ where: { id: spec.id } });
    if (existing) {
      await db.gamePlan.update({ where: { id: spec.id }, data });
      baselineUpdated++;
    } else {
      await db.gamePlan.create({ data: { id: spec.id, ...data } });
      baselineCreated++;
    }
  }

  // ── Step 3: add the new 4th (or 3rd+4th) tier for every family ───────────
  let tierCreated = 0;
  let tierUpdated = 0;
  for (const spec of NEW_TIERS) {
    const basePlan = pickBasePlan(spec.ramMB);
    const osId = await pickOsTemplate(spec.gameFamily);
    // sortOrder: entry tiers sort before every existing tier (existing ones
    // are never renumbered — see the "only ADD tiers" rule above); top tiers
    // sort after every currently-active tier for this family, in the order
    // NEW_TIERS lists them (matters for cs2's two new top tiers).
    let sortOrder: number;
    if (spec.direction === "entry") {
      sortOrder = -1;
    } else {
      const agg = await db.gamePlan.aggregate({
        where: { gameFamily: spec.gameFamily, active: true, id: { not: spec.id } },
        _max: { sortOrder: true },
      });
      sortOrder = (agg._max.sortOrder ?? -1) + 1;
    }
    const data = {
      gameFamily: spec.gameFamily,
      name: spec.name,
      ramMB: spec.ramMB,
      cpuCores: spec.cpuCores,
      diskGB: spec.diskGB,
      slots: spec.slots,
      priceCents: spec.priceCents,
      introPriceCents: spec.introPriceCents,
      introTermMonths: null,
      termMonths: 1,
      basePlanId: basePlan.id,
      osTemplateId: osId,
      featured: false, // new tiers ship unfeatured; owner can promote after review
      active: true,
      sortOrder,
    };
    const existing = await db.gamePlan.findUnique({ where: { id: spec.id } });
    if (existing) {
      await db.gamePlan.update({ where: { id: spec.id }, data });
      tierUpdated++;
    } else {
      await db.gamePlan.create({ data: { id: spec.id, ...data } });
      tierCreated++;
    }
    console.log(
      `  ${spec.gameFamily.padEnd(16)} ${spec.name.padEnd(46)} → base=${basePlan.name} img=${osId ? "yes" : "auto"} sortOrder=${sortOrder}`,
    );
  }

  console.log(`\nOsTemplate rows created: ${osCreated}`);
  console.log(`Baseline (missing-family) tiers: ${baselineCreated} created, ${baselineUpdated} updated`);
  console.log(`New 4th-tier rows: ${tierCreated} created, ${tierUpdated} updated`);

  // ── Verify: every family now has exactly 4 active tiers ──────────────────
  const counts = await db.gamePlan.groupBy({
    by: ["gameFamily"],
    where: { active: true },
    _count: { _all: true },
  });
  const notFour = counts.filter((c) => c._count._all !== 4);
  console.log(`\nFamilies with active tiers: ${counts.length}`);
  if (notFour.length > 0) {
    console.log("Families NOT at exactly 4 active tiers:");
    for (const c of notFour) console.log(`  ${c.gameFamily}: ${c._count._all}`);
  } else {
    console.log("Every family has exactly 4 active tiers. ✔");
  }
}

main()
  .catch((e) => {
    console.error(e);
    process.exit(1);
  })
  .finally(async () => {
    await db.$disconnect();
  });

# Nxeon vs. the market — game catalogue gap analysis

Read-only research. No code or database changes made. Compiled 2026-09-27.

## 1. Method

1. **Nxeon's own catalogue** (source of truth): `sudo -u postgres psql -d nxeon -At -c 'select distinct "gameFamily" from "GamePlan" where active order by 1'` → **47 active families**, cross-referenced against `GAME_FAMILIES`/`GAME_DISPLAY` in `/root/nxeon-worktrees/game-plans/lib/games.ts` for display names. (Plutonium T4/T5/T6/IW5 — community Call of Duty private-server hosting — exist in the codebase but are **not** in the 47 active `GamePlan` rows and are treated separately below as a specialty product, per that file's own comments explaining why it's excluded from the flagship catalogue.)
2. **Competitors**: fetched each host's own current games/homepage pages via WebFetch, 2026-09-27, supplemented by WebSearch where a page blocked the fetch (403) or 404'd. Every list below is what that host's own site showed today; source URL + "checked 2026-09-27" is given per host. Existing sourced facts (game *counts*, pricing, etc.) from `/root/nxeon-worktrees/marketing-nxm/app/nxm/_data/vs-hosts-data.ts` (also dated 2026-09-27) were reused, not contradicted.
3. **Demand data**: SteamDB/SteamCharts/Tracker.gg current + 24h-peak + all-time-peak concurrent players, via WebSearch (direct WebFetch of steamdb.info returned 403/Cloudflare block every time — noted per-fact). Every figure below has a source; anything I could not verify is marked **unknown**, never invented, per this codebase's own "never fabricate" rule (`CLAUDE.md`).
4. **Dedicated-server feasibility**: whether an official or well-established community dedicated-server tool/Docker image exists — a game with none of those can't be hosted regardless of demand.

## 1. Method

1. **Source data**: prod `nxeon` DB's 135 active `GamePlan` rows across 47
   families (2-3 tiers each today), read via `psql` (read-only). Staging
   (`nxeon_staging`) has the same 42 families but was missing 5 entirely
   (dayz, armareforger, cs16, ets2, ats — added here, see §4) and had 0-row
   "plutonium*" placeholder families that aren't part of prod's 47 and were
   left untouched.
2. **Sizing**: each new tier's RAM/CPU/disk is computed from
   `lib/game-player-recommend.ts`'s `GAME_PLAYER_CURVES` — the SAME fitted
   player→resource curve the live deploy wizard and the custom-plan slider
   already use — evaluated at a smaller or larger recommended player count
   than the family's existing floor/ceiling, then snapped to a "nice" RAM
   value (1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40 GB…).
3. **Direction (entry vs. top)**: for each family, both directions were
   computed and checked against two guardrails before picking one:
   - An **entry** tier (below the current floor) is only used if the curve's
     RAM at a smaller player count is meaningfully below (≥20%) the existing
     smallest tier's RAM AND rounds to a genuinely smaller "nice" value — i.e.
     the game can actually run there. Where it can't, or the result ties the
     current floor, a **top** tier (above the current ceiling) is added
     instead — exactly the brief's own fallback rule.
   - Families that only had 2 existing tiers (cs2, palworld, sons of the
     forest, terraria, the forest, valheim) get **both** an entry and a top —
     except **CS2**, which gets two top tiers instead: a 1 GB CS2 entry would
     sit below Source 2's real floor (the existing 2 GB tier is already that
     floor), so per the brief's own instruction ("if a game can't go lower,
     add two tiers above instead") it gets two top tiers.
4. **Price**: fit as a linear regression of `priceCents` vs. RAM(GB) over the
   family's OWN existing active tiers — i.e. literally extrapolating that
   family's established $/GB curve, per the brief. Two guardrails on top of
   the raw fit:
   - **Entry tiers are floored** at the smallest existing tier's own $/GB
     rate (×1.05) — a 2-3-point linear fit can go negative-intercept and
     imply a SMALLER tier costs less per GB than a bigger one, which is
     economically backwards and was caught happening for 7 families (ark,
     arkasa, conan, dst, l4d2, mordhau, soulmask, unturned) before this floor
     was added.
   - **Top-tier disk never shrinks**: the generic per-player disk curve
     undershoots reality for several families whose existing disk sizes are
     driven by fixed content (workshop maps, world saves), not linearly by
     player count — disk is floored at the existing top tier's own
     disk-per-RAM-GB ratio, scaled up proportionally.
   - Where a family has intro pricing (`introPriceCents`) on its existing
     tiers, the new tier's intro is set at that family's average
     intro:regular ratio. Where a family currently has NO intro pricing at
     all (the wave 10/11 additions — armareforger, ats, cs16, dayz, ets2),
     the new tier stays introPriceCents: null too, for consistency.
5. **Recommended players (`slots`)**: set to the SAME player count the tier's
   RAM was sized for — i.e. it's a readout of the curve, not a separate
   number, framed in the UI as "Sized for ~N players" (see §0).
6. **Five placeholder-curve families — hand-adjusted, not pure curve-fit**:
   `lib/game-player-recommend.ts`'s own doc comment flags **abioticfactor,
   dragonwilds, sunkenland, corekeeper, icarus** as "Wave 3 SCAFFOLD… NOT
   least-squares fits… MUST be re-fit before these games go live." Two of the
   five (icarus, sunkenland) produced unusable raw output from the generic
   formula — icarus's naive top candidate landed exactly on its existing top
   tier's RAM (no real new tier), and sunkenland's implied a ~3x price jump
   for a proportionally small player-count increase. Those two were
   hand-sized instead, cross-checked against the family's own organic
   tier-to-tier RAM/price progression (the same "own curve" principle,
   applied by hand where the automated curve is documented as unreliable).
   The other three (abioticfactor, dragonwilds, corekeeper) happened to
   produce numbers that already matched their own organic progression, so
   they were kept as computed.
7. **Competitor cross-check** (not the primary pricing driver — the family's
   own curve is — but a sanity bound): using the sourced 2026-09-27 figures
   already compiled in `/root/nxeon-worktrees/marketing-nxm/app/nxm/_data/vs-hosts-data.ts`
   for Minecraft (the one game every competitor prices consistently, so it's
   the only clean apples-to-apples benchmark):

   | Host | $/GB (their listed price) |
   |---|---|
   | Sparked Host (Budget line) | $1.00 |
   | PebbleHost (Budget line) | $1.00 |
   | GGServers (Standard) | $3.00 |
   | Shockbyte | $2.80 |
   | GPORTAL | $3.07 (intro $2.30) |
   | Apex Hosting | $3.50–3.75 (intro lower) |
   | Host Havoc | $3.75–5.00 |
   | Nitrado | $8.09 |
   | **Nxeon Minecraft today** | **$2.88–3.59** (8 GB / 2 GB) |
   | **Nxeon Minecraft entry (NEW)** | **$4.05** (1.5 GB) |

   Nxeon already sits in the middle of the market on Minecraft, and every
   other family's new tiers were priced by extending that SAME family's own
   established rate (per the brief), which keeps them in a comparable band —
   nothing in the new-tier table below is priced above ~2x any competitor
   figure gathered for that class of game.

METHOD

## 5. Staging vs. prod price note (read before eyeballing $/GB on staging)

Staging's pre-existing (untouched) tiers are priced from an **older, lower**
pricing era than prod's current live prices — e.g. staging's Minecraft 2 GB
tier is $4.99 vs. prod's current $7.18 for the identical spec (staging's base
VPS `Plan` rows are similarly ~30% cheaper across the board). This is a
pre-existing divergence between the two databases, unrelated to this change —
nothing here touched staging's existing tiers or its `Plan` table.

Every NEW tier's price in this proposal was fit against **prod's** real,
current $/GB curve (the correct source of truth for a production-bound
pricing decision), then seeded onto staging verbatim. That means on staging
today, a new tier's price will look disproportionately high next to its
staging siblings — that's expected and is a staging-data-freshness artifact,
not a pricing bug. Judge the numbers in the per-family tables above against
each other and against prod's existing column, not against what's rendered
live on the staging site right now.

## 6. Families where a clean 4-tier ladder needed a judgment call

- **CS2**: two tiers ABOVE the current ceiling instead of one entry + one top
  — a 1 GB entry would sit below Source 2's real minimum (the existing 2 GB
  tier is already that floor). See §1.3.
- **ATS / ETS2**: both games hard-cap at 8 players in-engine (SCS's own
  official ceiling — see `lib/game-player-recommend.ts`'s comment on these two
  curves), so a 4th tier can't be "more players." It's framed instead as more
  RAM/disk headroom for a heavier DLC-map/mod/AI-traffic convoy — "Heavy
  Modded Convoy" — continuing the existing Solo/Standard/Modded naming
  convention, same recommended player count (8) as the existing top tier.
- **Core Keeper**: same headroom framing (a "Modded" tier at more RAM/disk,
  same ~8 recommended players as the existing top) — its own curve is one of
  the five flagged placeholders (see §1.6) and its raw player-scaled output
  didn't clear either the entry or the natural top threshold.
- **Icarus, Sunkenland**: hand-sized rather than curve-computed — see §1.6.
- **Abiotic Factor, Dragonwilds**: also flagged placeholder-curve families,
  but their computed numbers already matched the family's own organic
  tier-to-tier progression, so no override was needed.

No family was left at fewer than 4 tiers — every one of the 47 got exactly
one more (two for the six that started with only 2).

## 7. To apply to production

After the owner reviews/adjusts prices in this document (and the actual
staging tiers, visible now at the staging site's game deploy pages):

```
DATABASE_URL="<prod DATABASE_URL from /opt/nxeon/.env>" npx tsx prisma/seed-gameplans-4tier.ts
```

**Do not run this against production without explicit sign-off** — it has
not been run there. It is idempotent (safe to re-run) and only ever inserts
new rows / updates rows it created itself (`gp4t-*` ids) — it never touches
an existing tier.

## 8. Files

- Seed script: `prisma/seed-gameplans-4tier.ts` (run against staging only so far)
- UI wording fix: `components/customer/GameDeployWizard.tsx` (3 spots, "Up to
  N players/slots" → "Sized for ~N players", matching `components/nx/DeployView.tsx`)
- This proposal: `/root/nxeon-competitive/plan-ladders.md`
- Docs: `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` §15 dated bullet added

## 5. Staging vs. prod price note (read before eyeballing $/GB on staging)

Staging's pre-existing (untouched) tiers are priced from an **older, lower**
pricing era than prod's current live prices — e.g. staging's Minecraft 2 GB
tier is $4.99 vs. prod's current $7.18 for the identical spec (staging's base
VPS `Plan` rows are similarly ~30% cheaper across the board). This is a
pre-existing divergence between the two databases, unrelated to this change —
nothing here touched staging's existing tiers or its `Plan` table.

Every NEW tier's price in this proposal was fit against **prod's** real,
current $/GB curve (the correct source of truth for a production-bound
pricing decision), then seeded onto staging verbatim. That means on staging
today, a new tier's price will look disproportionately high next to its
staging siblings — that's expected and is a staging-data-freshness artifact,
not a pricing bug. Judge the numbers in the per-family tables above against
each other and against prod's existing column, not against what's rendered
live on the staging site right now.

## 6. Families where a clean 4-tier ladder needed a judgment call

- **CS2**: two tiers ABOVE the current ceiling instead of one entry + one top
  — a 1 GB entry would sit below Source 2's real minimum (the existing 2 GB
  tier is already that floor). See §1.3.
- **ATS / ETS2**: both games hard-cap at 8 players in-engine (SCS's own
  official ceiling — see `lib/game-player-recommend.ts`'s comment on these two
  curves), so a 4th tier can't be "more players." It's framed instead as more
  RAM/disk headroom for a heavier DLC-map/mod/AI-traffic convoy — "Heavy
  Modded Convoy" — continuing the existing Solo/Standard/Modded naming
  convention, same recommended player count (8) as the existing top tier.
- **Core Keeper**: same headroom framing (a "Modded" tier at more RAM/disk,
  same ~8 recommended players as the existing top) — its own curve is one of
  the five flagged placeholders (see §1.6) and its raw player-scaled output
  didn't clear either the entry or the natural top threshold.
- **Icarus, Sunkenland**: hand-sized rather than curve-computed — see §1.6.
- **Abiotic Factor, Dragonwilds**: also flagged placeholder-curve families,
  but their computed numbers already matched the family's own organic
  tier-to-tier progression, so no override was needed.

No family was left at fewer than 4 tiers — every one of the 47 got exactly
one more (two for the six that started with only 2).

## Plans, terms and pricing

**What it does.** A `Plan` is a CPU/RAM/disk/bandwidth tier with one monthly price. A **term**
applies a commitment discount on top. A **promo** applies a seasonal discount on top of that.

Term ladder — `/opt/nxeon/lib/billing-terms.ts:9`:

| Term | `months` | Discount | $8.99/mo plan → effective |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monthly | 1 | 0% | $8.99/mo |
| Annual | 12 | 10% | $8.09/mo |
| Biennial | 24 | 15% | $7.64/mo |
| Triennial | 36 | 20% | $7.19/mo |

Domains have their own ladder (`DOMAIN_TERMS`, 1/2/3 years at 0/5/10%).

The three pricing functions, and this is the whole contract:

```
vpsTermPriceCents(monthly, months)   = round(monthly × months × (1 − disc))
                                       → what is CHARGED
vpsEffectiveMonthly(monthly, months) = round(termPrice / months)
                                       → what is DISPLAYED as "$/mo"
promoPriceCents(cents, promo)        = seasonal discount on top   lib/promotions.ts
```

Renewals bill `vpsTermPriceCents` **unchanged** — the promo applies to the first term only. That is
stated in the comment at `/opt/nxeon/lib/order.ts:199-201`, and the wizard's term cards now print
both numbers (`{total} first term · then {regTotal}`, `DeployWizard.tsx:816-825`) rather than the
first-term figure under a "billed every 1 yr" label. They used to print only the promo price, which
was wrong on 100% of orders, because `currentPromo()` never returns null.

**Entry points.** Term table and maths `/opt/nxeon/lib/billing-terms.ts` (`VPS_TERMS` at `:9`,
`vpsTermPriceCents` at `:21`); promo `/opt/nxeon/lib/promotions.ts` (`currentPromo` `:115`,
`promoPriceCents` `:139`, `deepestPromoPercent` `:152`); **what a renewal costs**
`/opt/nxeon/lib/renewal-charge.ts:43` — see the Renewals chapter, it is the only definition; admin
plan CRUD `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/plans`; catalog seed `/opt/nxeon/prisma/catalog.ts`. Guarded by
`/opt/nxeon/test/billing-terms.test.ts` and `/opt/nxeon/test/pricing-display-vs-charge.test.ts`.

**Data model.** `Plan` (`prisma/schema.prisma:253`): `slug`, `cpuCores`, `ramMB`, `diskGB`,
`bandwidthTB`, `priceCents`, `storageTier` (`nvme` | `hdd`), `active`, `sortOrder`. `GamePlan`
(`:777`) layers a game tier on top of a base `Plan`. `Server.termMonths` records which term was
bought.

**Failure mode that actually happened.** The wizard displayed $8.99 and charged $6.29 because the
promo was applied on one side only. Both sides now apply it — but by *duplication*, not by sharing
one function: `promoPriceCents` is reimplemented client-side in the wizard
(`components/customer/DeployWizard.tsx:154`) rather than imported.

**The card leg is now bound; the wallet leg is not.** `createOrderCheckout` stamps the whole quote
into Stripe metadata as `nxeonOrderPrice` (`lib/stripe.ts:109`), the confirm route parses it back
(`:264`) and `placeOrder` takes it as `sold` (`lib/order.ts:238`, applied at `:245-247`), so a card
order settles at the price it was **sold** at rather than at a price recomputed after the card has
cleared. `payAndDeploy`'s wallet-only branch calls `placeOrder(user, intent)` with no `sold`
(`lib/actions.ts:475`) and re-quotes from its own `new Date()`, so a promo boundary crossed between
the Review screen and the click still moves the number. That is the residual half of gap 26 in
Known gaps.

**Diagnosis.** For "I was charged the wrong amount": read the `Invoice.lineItems` (they spell out
term and promo), then re-run the maths by hand with `vpsTermPriceCents` and the promo that was live
at `Invoice.createdAt`. `AuditLog` action `server.order` records `plan=`, `term=`, `extraDisk=`.
